Absolutely. We are hard-wired to tend toward tribalism, pattern recognition where none exists, and the creation of deities to explain the currently unexplainable. There are valid evolutionary reasons for all of these, but they can also cause untold amounts of blowback -- as they have on many occasions.

Take, for example, the Polynesian belief that an earthquake means the Land God and the Sea God are fighting. This "explains" the likely tsunami to follow, and induces the people to head for high ground. Obviously this serves a survival function. However, if those same Polynesians were to go to war with another island because they believe in a different Land God and Sea God, this only serves to depopulate both islands. If they decide that someone must not study the cause of earthquakes or their connection to tsunamis because that would be violating the province of the gods, they are forfeiting an opportunity to maximize their own survival probability.

We're hardwired for these shortcuts because in a limited information scenario, such as most people have lived for most of history (and some still do), it works better than the alternative. However, add more information and those mechanisms fall apart because they weren't designed to filter all of that at once. Thus people will reject evidence that does not support the worldview they already possess, and plug their ears to prevent cognitive dissonance.

Instinct is good when you're under extreme time pressure. If there may be a tiger lurking behind that bush, you really don't have time to analyze the situation deeply. But when the situation requires long-term planning, these instincts can become quite counterproductive.
